cards.q: What is a distributed system?
cards.a: A group of computers that work together over a network and look like **one system** to the user. Opening Instagram may touch dozens of servers, but to you it is just "Instagram".

cards.q: What four things can happen to a message on the network?
cards.a: It can be **lost**, **late** (by milliseconds or by many seconds), **duplicated** because someone retried, or **out of order**.

cards.q: Why does "no reply" tell you nothing?
cards.a: The request may have been lost, the server may have done the work and the reply was lost, or it is just slow. All three look the same: silence. So use timeouts and retries, made safe with idempotency.

cards.q: What is a partial failure?
cards.a: Some parts fail while others keep working. Example: the order is saved, the payment failed, and nobody knows if the email went out. The data is half done. It is the hardest kind of failure.

cards.q: What two things do machines in a distributed system not share?
cards.a: A **clock**: each has its own and they drift, so timestamps can't show which event came first. **Memory**: to agree on anything, like who is leader or who holds a lock, they must send messages over the network.

cards.q: In an interview, what should you say whenever you draw an arrow between two services?
cards.a: What happens when that call fails or times out. Example: "A timeout doesn't tell us whether the charge happened, so we retry with an idempotency key."

cards.q: What do the C, A and P in CAP mean?
cards.a: **Consistency:** every read gets the newest data. **Availability:** every request gets an answer, not an error. **Partition tolerance:** the system keeps working when the network between machines breaks.

cards.q: Why is the real CAP choice between C and A?
cards.a: Network breaks (partitions) **will** happen, so P is not optional. The real question is: when the network breaks, do you pick consistency or availability?

cards.q: During a network break, what does a "pick C" copy do vs a "pick A" copy?
cards.a: **Pick C:** it returns an error, or waits, until it can be sure it has the newest data. **Pick A:** it answers right away, maybe with old data, like the old name "Rob" instead of the new "Bob".

cards.q: What question helps you choose between C and A?
cards.a: "What is worse for the user: old data for a few seconds, or an error?" Money, booking the last seat and stock at checkout → consistency. Likes, feeds, comments and profiles → availability.

cards.q: What does PACELC mean, and who proposed it?
cards.a: **If** there is a **P**artition, choose **A**vailability or **C**onsistency. **E**lse (normal times), choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency. Proposed by Daniel Abadi (first in 2010, fully in a 2012 article).

cards.q: Why is there a latency vs consistency trade-off even when nothing is broken?
cards.a: Keeping copies in sync means waiting for the other copies to confirm, and that wait is added to **every write**. Like a bank branch that phones the other branch before every withdrawal: always right, but every customer waits.

cards.q: What is a consistency model?
cards.a: The promise a system makes about **what a reader sees** while copies (replicas) catch up after a write. A stronger promise is easier to build on, but slower and fails more often during network problems.

cards.q: What is strong consistency, and how is it built?
cards.a: Every read sees the latest write, as if there were only one copy (formally, **linearizability**). It is built by sending every read and write to one leader, or with a consensus algorithm like Raft.

cards.q: What does eventual consistency promise, and what doesn't it promise?
cards.a: If writes stop, all copies become the same eventually. There is no promise about exactly when, so a reader may see old data until then. In return, it is fast and keeps working during network problems.

cards.q: What does read-your-writes prevent, and how do you fix it with replicas?
cards.a: You edit your bio, refresh and see the old bio. Fix: remember the user's last write time, and for a short time after (like 10 seconds) send their reads to the primary. Or show the change from the write's response.

cards.q: What are N, W and R in a quorum, and which rule matters?
cards.a: **N** = copies of the data, **W** = copies that must confirm a write, **R** = copies asked on a read. If **R + W is greater than N**, the read and write copies overlap by at least one, so one answer has the newest value.

cards.q: How do you pick a consistency level for each feature?
cards.a: Ask "what breaks if this read is a few seconds old?" Money and bookings: strong. Your own profile: read-your-writes. Comments: causal. Likes and feeds: eventual. One app mixing levels is normal.

cards.q: ACID vs BASE: what does each put first?
cards.a: **ACID** puts correct data first, like one central bank counter. **BASE** puts always answering first, like branch shops that keep their own notebooks and match them up later.

cards.q: How is ACID's C different from CAP's C?
cards.a: ACID's C means the data always follows **your rules**, like "a balance is never negative". CAP's C means every reader sees the **newest write**. Same letter, different ideas.

cards.q: What does BASE stand for?
cards.a: **Basically Available:** always answers, even if data is a little old. **Soft state:** data may still be changing in the background while copies catch up. **Eventually consistent:** with no new writes, all copies become the same.

cards.q: What do a single-primary SQL setup and a BASE system usually do when the network breaks?
cards.a: The single-primary SQL setup usually refuses requests rather than give old data: CAP's **C**. BASE systems keep answering: CAP's **A**. ACID itself says nothing about copies: a read replica can still return old data.

cards.q: How do you choose between ACID and BASE?
cards.a: Would old or wrong data cost money or break a rule? ACID. Huge write volume, many regions, must never go down? BASE. Otherwise, start with ACID (PostgreSQL): it is simpler to build on.

cards.q: What is a distributed transaction, and why isn't one database transaction enough?
cards.a: One that spans many databases or services and still tries to be all-or-nothing. With microservices, each service has its own database, and one database's transaction can't see or undo what another did.

cards.q: What is two-phase commit (2PC)?
cards.a: A **coordinator** first asks every **participant** (each database) if it can commit: the vote. Then it announces one decision that everyone follows. Like a wedding: both say "I do", then the officiant pronounces them married.

cards.q: What does a "yes" vote in 2PC promise?
cards.a: "I am ready, and I will commit if you tell me to, even if I crash and restart." Once it votes yes, it can't change its mind: it keeps its locks and waits for the decision.

cards.q: What is blocking in 2PC?
cards.a: The coordinator crashes after the votes but before deciding. Participants can't commit (someone may have voted no) or abort (someone may have been told to commit), so they wait, holding locks.

cards.q: Besides blocking, what are the problems with 2PC?
cards.a: It is slow: two rounds of messages, disk writes and locks held, as slow as the slowest participant. Everyone must be up. And everyone must support it: you can't "prepare" an email and then un-send it.

cards.q: Why do microservice teams usually pick a saga over 2PC?
cards.a: 2PC holds locks across services, gets stuck if the coordinator dies, and outside APIs can't take part. In a saga, each step commits and releases right away, and failures are undone with compensating actions.

cards.q: What is a saga?
cards.a: A long flow split into steps. Each step is a local transaction in one service that **commits right away**. If a later step fails, undo steps run for the earlier ones, in **reverse order**.

cards.q: What price do you pay for using a saga?
cards.a: For a short time the system is **in between** (flight booked, hotel not yet), and others can see it: sagas don't give ACID's isolation. Use clear statuses like `PENDING`, `CONFIRMED` and `CANCELLED`.

cards.q: What is a compensating action?
cards.a: The official name for an undo step. It is a **new action, not an eraser**: you refund a payment, you don't delete it. Both records stay, which is good for audits.

cards.q: Where should steps that can't be undone go in a saga?
cards.a: **Last**, after everything that might fail. You can't un-send an email or un-ship a parcel. Since there is no undo, retry them with an idempotency key until they work.

cards.q: What is choreography in a saga?
cards.a: Nobody is in charge: each service listens for events, does its step and publishes a new event. Simple for short flows, but answering "where is order 42 right now?" means reading every service's logs.

cards.q: What is orchestration in a saga?
cards.a: One service, the **orchestrator**, tells each service what to do, step by step, and remembers where the saga is. The whole flow is in one place, so it is usually easier to explain and to debug.

cards.q: What is the dual write problem?
cards.a: A service must save data in its database **and** send an event to a broker like Kafka. These are two different systems, and no single transaction covers both.

cards.q: Save-then-send vs send-then-save: what can go wrong?
cards.a: **Save, then send:** the app crashes, or Kafka is down, before sending, so the event is lost. **Send, then save:** the save fails, so other services act on an order that doesn't exist.

cards.q: What is the outbox pattern?
cards.a: Write the event into an `outbox` table in the **same database and same transaction** as the data. Both are saved, or neither is. A separate relay publishes the event later.

cards.q: Polling relay vs log-reading (CDC) relay?
cards.a: **Polling:** every second or so, read rows where `sent_at` is empty. Simple and works with any database, but adds queries and a small delay. **CDC:** read the database's change log. Fast, no polling, but needs a tool like Debezium.

cards.q: Why does the outbox give at-least-once delivery?
cards.a: The relay can crash **after** publishing an event but **before** marking it sent. After a restart it sees the row as unsent and publishes it again. Events are never lost, but can arrive twice.

cards.q: How does the outbox keep one order's events in order?
cards.a: The relay sends rows in `seq` order (a `BIGSERIAL` set on insert) and uses `aggregate_id` (the order ID) as the Kafka key, so all events for one order go to the same partition. Not `created_at`: `now()` is when the transaction started, not when it was saved.

cards.q: What is Change Data Capture (CDC)?
cards.a: It watches a database and turns **every insert, update and delete into an event**. The app writes to one place only, and search, caches and reports follow the stream of changes.

cards.q: Why not have the app update both the database and the search index itself?
cards.a: That is a dual write. If the second write fails, they disagree forever. Racing updates can reach search in the wrong order. And every new system means more app code. With CDC, the database's log decides the order.

cards.q: How does log-based CDC work?
cards.a: Before changing data, a database writes each change to an append-only log (PostgreSQL's WAL, MySQL's binlog). A CDC tool reads that log like one more replica and turns each entry into an event.

cards.q: Polling vs triggers vs log-based CDC?
cards.a: **Polling** on `updated_at` misses deletes and quick changes, and adds load. **Triggers** slow down every write. **Log-based** catches everything, in order, with little extra load: the usual choice.

cards.q: Why should CDC consumers upsert by ID?
cards.a: Events are delivered at least once, so the same change can come twice. Writing by ID (insert, or update if it exists) means a repeat does no harm.

cards.q: How does raw CDC turn your tables into an API, and what is the fix?
cards.a: Other teams depend on your column names, so renaming a column can break them. Fix: let CDC read only the **outbox table**, so others see designed events like `OrderPlaced`, not raw rows.

cards.q: What is a distributed lock, and why isn't an in-memory lock enough?
cards.a: On one server, a lock in memory (a mutex) works. But servers can't see each other's memory, so the lock must live in a **shared place** every server can reach, like Redis, etcd or ZooKeeper.

cards.q: Lock for saving work vs lock for correctness: what do you use?
cards.a: **Saving work** (two holders just waste effort): a simple Redis lock is fine. **Correctness** (two holders break data or move money twice): etcd or ZooKeeper **plus fencing tokens**.

cards.q: How do you release a Redis lock safely?
cards.a: Delete the key **only if it still holds your token**, or you may delete a lock that has passed to someone else. Do the check and the delete in one step, with a small Lua script.

cards.q: Why must a distributed lock expire?
cards.a: If the holder crashes, a lock with no timeout stays forever, and nobody can ever do the job again. A lock with an expiry time is called a **lease**.

cards.q: How can a lock holder lose its lock without knowing it?
cards.a: It freezes, say in a long GC pause, a paused VM or a slow network. Its lease expires and another worker takes the lock. Then the first one wakes up **still believing it holds the lock**.

cards.q: What is a fencing token?
cards.a: A number that always goes up each time the lock is given out (33, then 34). The worker sends it with every write, and storage **rejects older tokens**. etcd and ZooKeeper can give one; a plain Redis lock doesn't.

cards.q: Leader election vs consensus?
cards.a: **Leader election:** a group of servers picks one leader to make decisions. **Consensus:** servers agree on the same value, like who the leader is or the order of writes, even when some crash or messages are lost.

cards.q: Why does a majority vote stop two leaders from winning?
cards.a: Any two majorities of the same group always share at least one server. That server can't vote for two different leaders in the same election, so only one can win.

cards.q: Why do consensus groups use 3 or 5 servers?
cards.a: 3 servers can lose 1, and 5 can lose 2. 4 servers can still lose only 1, like 3, so groups almost always use an **odd** number.

cards.q: How does a Raft election work?
cards.a: A follower that hears no heartbeat for a random wait becomes a candidate: term + 1, votes for itself, asks for votes. Each server gives one vote per term, only to a candidate at least as up to date. A majority wins.

cards.q: What is split brain, and why can't a cut-off old leader cause it in Raft?
cards.a: Split brain is **two leaders** both accepting writes. If a network split leaves the old leader with only 2 of 5 servers, it has no majority, so it can't commit any write. Only the bigger side elects a new leader and makes progress.

cards.q: How do you do leader election in practice?
cards.a: Use **etcd** or **ZooKeeper**; don't build your own. Every candidate tries to create the same key, tied to a lease or session, and the first one wins. The key disappears if the holder dies, and the others watch it and try again.

cards.q: Why can't you sort events from different servers by timestamp?
cards.a: Every server has its own clock, and no two clocks agree exactly. So sorting by timestamp does not reliably give the real order of events on different machines.

cards.q: Why is "last write wins" dangerous with real server clocks?
cards.a: If one server's clock is fast, its older write gets the bigger timestamp. The write that really came later is **silently thrown away**.

cards.q: Wall clock vs monotonic clock: when do you use each?
cards.a: **Wall clock:** a date and time, for showing time to people and for log lines; it can jump forward or back. **Monotonic clock:** only moves forward; use it to measure durations and timeouts.

cards.q: How accurate is NTP, and what does that mean for timestamps?
cards.a: Tens of milliseconds over the internet, better than a millisecond on a good local network, never perfect. So use timestamps to show time to people and for rough order, not to decide which write wins.

cards.q: What does a Lamport clock promise, and what can't it tell you?
cards.a: If X caused Y, X's number is smaller. But a smaller number does **not** prove X caused Y: the events may be **concurrent**, unaware of each other. Ties are broken with `(counter, serverId)`.

cards.q: What can a vector clock do that a Lamport clock can't, and at what cost?
cards.a: It can spot **concurrent** writes, which are real conflicts. The cost: one counter per server, so the list grows with every server that writes. It is used where conflict detection matters, like leaderless databases.

cards.q: What are the limits of auto-increment IDs?
cards.a: Perfect on one database, but **sharding breaks it**: each database counts from 1. One central counter is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. And the IDs are easy to guess and leak business numbers.

cards.q: Why do random IDs slow down database inserts?
cards.a: An index is kept **sorted**. A random ID is squeezed in somewhere in the middle, touching a different page each time. A time-sorted ID always goes at the end. So UUID v7 is usually better than v4 for primary keys.

cards.q: What are the parts of a 64-bit Snowflake ID?
cards.a: **1** sign bit (always 0) + **41** bits of timestamp (ms since a chosen epoch, about 69 years) + **10** bits of machine ID (1,024 servers) + **12** bits of sequence (4,096 per ms).

cards.q: What must you watch out for with Snowflake IDs?
cards.a: Machine IDs must be unique. If the clock moves backward, IDs could repeat, so it refuses to make IDs until the clock catches up. And IDs made in the same millisecond on different servers are only roughly sorted.

cards.q: What are counter ranges, and what are their tradeoffs?
cards.a: A central service hands each server a **block**, like 1 to 1,000, and it counts locally until the block runs out. Good: short numbers, one call per block. Bad: gaps after a restart, and IDs aren't in time order.

cards.q: Which ID method fits which situation?
cards.a: One database, small app: **auto-increment**. No coordination: **UUID** (v7 for a database key). 64-bit, time-sorted, huge scale: **Snowflake**. Short codes, like short links: **counter ranges**.

cards.q: What is CQRS?
cards.a: **Command Query Responsibility Segregation**: use one model to change data (commands) and a different model to read it (queries).

cards.q: Why is one model for reads and writes not always enough?
cards.a: Clean, normalized tables are best for writing but often bad for reading. A "My orders" page needs a big join on every view, search needs full-text matching, and dashboards need totals that are slow to calculate.

cards.q: What are a read model and a projector?
cards.a: A **read model** (or projection, or view) is data already shaped for a screen, like one document per order with names and pictures inside, so no joins. A **projector** is a small worker that keeps it up to date.

cards.q: How do you keep a CQRS read model in sync?
cards.a: With **events** from the write side (published safely with the outbox), with **CDC** reading the write database's log, or with **event sourcing**, where every view is built from the events.

cards.q: What is the catch with the CQRS read side?
cards.a: It **lags**: it updates a moment after the write, so a new order may not be in "My orders" yet. Show it straight from the command's response, or read that user's data from the write side for a few seconds.

cards.q: When is CQRS worth it, and when not?
cards.a: Worth it when reads and writes differ a lot in shape or volume, or you need several views like search, feeds and dashboards. Not for simple CRUD or a small team. Use it for one part of a system, not the whole app.

cards.q: What is event sourcing?
cards.a: Storing every change as an **event** in an append-only event log. Events are never changed or deleted, and the current state is worked out by **replaying** them in order, like adding up a bank passbook.

cards.q: Why is reading hard with event sourcing, and what is the fix?
cards.a: The event store is great for "all events for account 42", but bad for "all accounts with a balance over 1,000". So it is almost always paired with **CQRS**: projectors build ready-made read views.

cards.q: What is a snapshot in event sourcing?
cards.a: Every so often, say every 100 events, you save the state at that point. To load, read the latest snapshot and replay only the events after it, so replays stay fast.

cards.q: What are the good sides of event sourcing?
cards.a: Full history for free (a built-in audit log), time travel to any past state, replaying events to reproduce a bug, building new views from all past events, and fast writes that just add to the end.

cards.q: What are the bad sides of event sourcing?
cards.a: It is more complex, queries need separate read views, old events must stay readable forever (**versioning**), deleting data is hard, the read side lags a little, and replays get slow without snapshots.

cards.q: When is event sourcing a good fit, and when not?
cards.a: Good for money and ledgers, accounting, orders with many status changes, and anything that needs a full audit trail. Not for simple CRUD screens. Use it for the one part of a system that needs history.
